source_file: zhihu_移民加拿大有哪些攻略.txt

heuristics.rule: If you can qualify for LMIA job offer + EE, don't use provincial nomination
heuristics.condition: When an applicant has CRS score around 440-450 and can obtain a legitimate LMIA job offer (NOC 0/A/B)
heuristics.action: Use EE federal pathway directly rather than provincial nomination routes
heuristics.because: Provincial nomination adds an extra layer of process at the provincial level, lengthening total timeline and introducing more complexity and potential failure points, with no benefit over direct EE if LMIA job offer is available

heuristics.rule: Prepare WES credential evaluation early — do not wait for EE invitation
heuristics.condition: When an applicant with foreign credentials is planning to apply via federal EE
heuristics.action: Start WES credential evaluation process before receiving ITA
heuristics.because: After receiving ITA, document submission window was shortened from 90 days to 60 days (as of June 26, 2018), and WES evaluation alone can take up to 2 months

heuristics.rule: Manitoba PNP is viable even with out-of-province study/work penalty if base score is high enough
heuristics.condition: When an applicant studied or worked outside Manitoba before coming to Manitoba
heuristics.action: Still apply to Manitoba PNP — the -100 points per out-of-province factor is offset by the 500-point employer continuity bonus
heuristics.because: Historical invitation scores dropped as low as 567-585, meaning even after -200 points deduction for out-of-province study AND work, most applicants with Manitoba employer still exceed the threshold

heuristics.rule: For Manitoba PNP, working for the same Manitoba employer for 6+ months (local grad) or 1+ year (out-of-province grad) is the single most important factor
heuristics.condition: When a student is planning immigration pathway through Manitoba
heuristics.action: Prioritize finding and retaining a legitimate Manitoba employer over optimizing other scoring factors
heuristics.because: The Manitoba employer continuity factor adds 500 points — the single largest scoring component by far, making it the decisive variable in EOI scoring

heuristics.rule: Never accept a provincial nomination offer that promises permanent residency without first entering Canada to work
heuristics.condition: When a provincial nomination immigration company claims you can obtain PR and then land in Canada afterward
heuristics.action: Reject the offer and walk away
heuristics.because: No provincial nomination program today allows land-after-PR; federal officials will question the authenticity of the job if the applicant never worked during the 2-year provincial nomination to PR window, and provincial nomination can be revoked

decision_factors.factor: CRS score threshold relative to current draw levels
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether federal EE is a viable pathway at all, or whether alternative routes (PNP, LMIA job offer boost) are necessary
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate personal CRS score using official IRCC calculator; compare against last 10-20 draw scores for relevant category (all-program vs CEC draws)

decision_factors.factor: Whether the job offer and employer are genuinely legitimate and background-matched
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Immigration officers verify employer authenticity and applicant-role fit; mismatched or fabricated offers are investigated and can result in permanent inadmissibility
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask: does the applicant's educational and work background plausibly match the offered role? Is the employer in a region/industry where recruiting locally is genuinely difficult? Can the applicant answer detailed questions about the workplace?

decision_factors.factor: Province of study and work (Manitoba vs. other provinces)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Manitoba PNP awards 500 points for working with a Manitoba employer, while penalizes -100 per out-of-province study or work experience; studying/working in Ontario or BC carries no equivalent provincial bonus
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check applicant's current province of study/work and intended province of settlement; calculate EOI score with and without penalty

decision_factors.factor: Whether applicant has genuine entrepreneurial or self-employment background
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Federal SUV and self-employed programs are only viable for applicants whose backgrounds are credible to immigration officers; mismatch leads to rejection or multi-year delays
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Does the applicant have verifiable prior startup/business management experience? Does the business plan align with actual skills? Would an immigration officer find the claim credible?

decision_factors.why_it_matters: As of June 2017, French proficiency at NCLC 7 or above adds 15 bonus points to federal EE CRS score
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check whether applicant has or can realistically obtain NCLC 7 French; compare marginal cost of French study against value of 15 CRS points

decision_factors.factor: Having a sibling who is a Canadian citizen or PR, aged 18+
decision_factors.why_it_matters: As of June 6, 2017, having a qualifying sibling in Canada adds 15 bonus points to EE CRS score
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Verify sibling's status and age; claim in Express Entry profile

decision_factors.factor: Canadian education duration (1-2 years vs. 3+ years)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Post-November 2016 EE update: 1-2 years of Canadian study adds 15 CRS points; 3+ years adds 30 points
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check length of Canadian credential against this threshold; may influence program length decision for prospective students

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Purchasing an LMIA job offer from a high-volume immigration company
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: High-volume LMIA sellers are already on IRCC radar; if investigated, the fraud attaches to the applicant not the company, resulting in permanent inadmissibility
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Applicants who prioritize cost savings or choose large-scale immigration brokers over boutique firms with genuine employer relationships

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Applying for caregiver immigration pathway (Home Child Care Provider / Home Support Worker)
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The open but occupation-restricted work permit means any non-caregiving work is illegal; immigration officers conduct detailed household-specific interviews, and inability to answer specific questions about the home environment immediately reveals fake employment
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Applicants with strong educational backgrounds who are placed into caregiver roles by immigration companies without genuine employer matching

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Pursuing Atlantic Immigration Program with a purchased job offer without genuinely working
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: IRCC specifically scrutinizes Chinese applicants in this program; officers verify detailed job and company knowledge; getting caught results in removal and ban from future applications
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Applicants with polished white-collar backgrounds taking low-skilled Atlantic region offers that don't match their profile

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing provincial entrepreneur/investor immigration over federal SUV
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Provincial entrepreneur programs require meeting performance milestones (investment amounts, local hiring, profitability) over a 2-year operating period; business failure or underperformance can result in nomination revocation even after years of compliance effort
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Applicants who lack genuine business operational experience but are sold provincial entrepreneur immigration as a 'lower barrier' alternative

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing Manitoba PNP pathway via a college in another province then relocating
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Out-of-province study deducts 100 points; out-of-province work deducts another 100 points — total -200 penalty still survivable given 500-point employer bonus, but many applicants don't realize the penalty exists until after enrollment decisions are made
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who chose Ontario or BC colleges for quality reasons and then try to redirect to Manitoba for immigration purposes

failure_patterns.pattern: Purchasing batch-produced LMIA job offers from high-volume immigration companies
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Price anchoring and false safety in numbers — applicants reason that if a company does hundreds of these cases per year, it must be legitimate and safe
failure_patterns.consequence: IRCC flags bulk LMIA sellers; applications linked to known fraudulent employers are denied, and applicants receive misrepresentation findings that can result in 5-year bans
warning_signs: Immigration company claims to process hundreds or thousands of LMIA clients per year
Job offer price is significantly below market (below 150,000 CAD)
Company cannot explain specific employer background or provide verifiable employer references

failure_patterns.pattern: Applying for caregiver or Atlantic immigration with a profile that obviously doesn't match the role
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Applicants focus on meeting the minimum threshold requirements on paper, not on whether the overall profile is credible to an immigration officer
failure_patterns.consequence: Application flagged for detailed verification interview; applicant cannot answer specific questions about their supposed employer or work environment; application rejected with potential misrepresentation finding
warning_signs: Applicant has graduate degree or white-collar professional background
Job offer is for NOC C/D category role with no plausible connection to applicant's history
Immigration company does not ask detailed questions about applicant's work history before suggesting the program

failure_patterns.pattern: Pursuing provincial entrepreneur immigration without genuine business operational capability
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Applicants are told the program has low barriers and that local service providers will handle operations; they underestimate the requirement for genuine personal involvement and milestone achievement
failure_patterns.consequence: Failure to meet investment, hiring, or profitability commitments in the performance agreement; provincial nomination revoked after 2+ years of time and money spent
warning_signs: Immigration company promises 'full management service' with no need for personal involvement
Applicant has no prior business ownership or management experience
Program fee is unusually low for what is promised

failure_patterns.pattern: Over-relying on federal EE as the only pathway without calculating actual CRS score first
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: EE is the most publicly discussed pathway; applicants assume that meeting minimum eligibility thresholds means being competitive in draws
failure_patterns.consequence: Applicants enter the EE pool with scores of 410-440 and wait indefinitely while draw cutoffs remain above 470-490 for all-program draws; lose years of optimal immigration window age points
warning_signs: Applicant has not calculated their actual CRS score before committing to the EE pathway
Applicant conflates 'eligible for EE pool' with 'likely to receive ITA'

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting startup visa / self-employed program from immigration companies without verifying the quality of the supporting organization
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Applicants cannot distinguish between Tier 1 designated organizations (e.g., CDL, GTAN) and weak incubators; immigration companies exploit this information asymmetry
failure_patterns.consequence: Application fails at IRCC review stage despite paying full fees; in worst cases, immigration company collects deposit then delays or disappears without delivering the support letter
warning_signs: Company cannot name the specific designated organization that will issue the support letter
Support letter comes from an obscure incubator with no verifiable track record
Company does not offer contractual protection allowing withdrawal if team composition is unsatisfactory

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your actual calculated CRS score right now?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether federal EE is viable, whether LMIA job offer boost is needed, or whether provincial nomination is the only realistic pathway
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If above 490: consider direct EE application; if 440-490: explore LMIA job offer options; if below 440: evaluate provincial nomination or other federal programs
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Calculate score immediately using IRCC tool before committing to any pathway — all subsequent advice is meaningless without this number

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the immigration company you're considering claim to process hundreds or thousands of similar cases per year?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the company is running a high-volume, batch-processed operation that is likely using weak or fabricated employer relationships
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Treat as a red flag; programs requiring genuine employer matching (LMIA, Atlantic, caregiver, provincial entrepreneur) cannot be legitimately scaled to hundreds of clients per year
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Still verify employer authenticity and company track record independently

diagnostic_questions.question: Does your educational background and work history plausibly match the job offer being arranged for you?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the application will survive IRCC officer scrutiny on the role-applicant fit dimension
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Application has a credible foundation; proceed with verifying employer authenticity
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: High risk of detailed investigation and rejection; reconsider whether this pathway is appropriate regardless of technical eligibility

diagnostic_questions.question: If applying via Manitoba PNP: did you study or work outside Manitoba before coming to Manitoba?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the -100 point penalty per out-of-province factor applies, and whether total EOI score still clears historical invitation thresholds
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Calculate total score after penalty; as long as Manitoba employer 500-point bonus applies, most applicants still qualify based on historical draw data
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: No penalty applies; score calculation is straightforward

diagnostic_questions.question: For SUV applicants: what specific designated organization will issue your support letter, and what is that organization's track record with IRCC approvals?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the core bottleneck of the startup visa — the quality of the support letter source — is genuinely solved
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Verify the organization is on IRCC's current designated list and has a verifiable approval history
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The application is not ready to proceed; do not pay fees until this is answered concretely

industry_realities.common_belief: Canada still has an investor immigration program where you invest money and directly receive permanent residency
industry_realities.actual_reality: The Quebec investor immigration program (the last pure investment-for-PR program) closed in 2019. All current Canadian pathways require genuine work, business operation, or skills-based competition — there is no invest-and-receive-PR route
industry_realities.implication: Applicants marketed 'investor immigration' products should immediately question what they are actually being sold, as the product category no longer exists at the federal level

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting a provincial nomination means you have essentially completed the immigration process
industry_realities.actual_reality: Provincial nomination is only the first half; federal permanent residency application still takes 1.5-2 years after nomination, and the nominated person must continue working in the province during this period or risk having the nomination reviewed
industry_realities.implication: Applicants must plan for 3-4 total years of Canadian residence and genuine work, not just the time to obtain the provincial nomination letter

industry_realities.common_belief: LMIA job offers are a reliable way to add points to EE CRS score
industry_realities.actual_reality: As of the 2025 update referenced in the post, IRCC removed LMIA-based CRS score additions, eliminating one of the main paid pathways to boost scores. The EE system is now more purely merit-based
industry_realities.implication: Applicants who were planning to purchase LMIA job offers specifically to boost CRS score (rather than as a genuine employment arrangement) need to reassess their strategy entirely

industry_realities.common_belief: Low-barrier immigration programs (caregiver, Atlantic Immigration Program) are safe choices for applicants who don't meet higher-tier program requirements
industry_realities.actual_reality: Low-barrier programs attract heavier IRCC scrutiny precisely because they are low-barrier; IRCC has specifically increased verification intensity for Chinese applicants in Atlantic Immigration Program and caregivers after widespread abuse
industry_realities.implication: A technically eligible application with a mismatched profile faces higher actual rejection risk in these programs than a competitive application in a harder program

industry_realities.common_belief: The EE pool score just needs to be above the minimum eligibility threshold (67 points for FSW) to have a reasonable chance of being drawn
industry_realities.actual_reality: Entering the EE pool and being competitive in draws are completely different thresholds. FSW applicants need CRS scores around 490-500+ to be drawn in all-program rounds, while minimum pool eligibility only requires 67 FSW points
industry_realities.implication: Many applicants spend months or years in the EE pool with no realistic chance of being drawn, when they should be exploring PNP or other alternatives from the start

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Looks at whether they technically meet the minimum eligibility requirements for a program and assumes that means it's viable
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Calculates actual competitive ranking within the program (CRS score vs. draw history, EOI score vs. invitation history) before committing to any pathway
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Meeting minimum eligibility and having a realistic chance of success are entirely different things in points-based systems; confusing the two leads to years of wasted waiting

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treats high client volume as a trust signal ('they must know what they're doing if they handle thousands of cases')
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treats high client volume as a red flag for programs requiring genuine employer matching, and asks specific questions about employer identity, support letter source, and Barrister resources for appeal
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Batch-processed immigration products are systematically detected and flagged by IRCC; the applicant bears all the consequences while the company retains the fees

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Sees provincial nomination as the finish line and calculates timeline to nomination letter
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treats provincial nomination as the midpoint and plans for an additional 1.5-2 years of genuine provincial work before federal PR is granted
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Applicants who don't plan for the post-nomination federal process, or who leave the province after nomination, risk having their nomination revoked

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Asks 'which program has the lowest requirements I can technically meet?'
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Asks 'which program will an IRCC officer find my application most credible given my actual background?'
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Technical eligibility and officer credibility assessment are separate filters; mismatched profiles in low-barrier programs face higher scrutiny and rejection rates than matched profiles in harder programs

community_misconceptions.misconception: Canada has an investor immigration program where you invest money and get permanent residency
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Investor immigration programs existed historically in Canada (including Quebec) and are still widely marketed by immigration companies; the concept of 'money = visa' is intuitive and has precedent
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: The Quebec investor immigration program closed in 2019. All federal and provincial programs now require genuine work, business operation, skills competition, or family ties — no pure investment-for-PR pathway exists
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Applicants pay immigration companies for products that don't exist or are misrepresented; they either lose money on undeliverable promises or are directed into fraudulent arrangements

community_misconceptions.misconception: Getting a provincial nomination means immigration is essentially done — you just wait for paperwork
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The nomination letter is a tangible milestone that feels decisive; the federal stage is framed as a formality by immigration companies incentivized to close the sale
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: After provincial nomination, applicants still need to complete federal PR application (1.5-2 years), must continue genuine employment in the nominated province, and nomination can be revoked if employment conditions change
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Applicants who stop working or leave the province after nomination face revocation; those who planned their finances around a shorter timeline run into serious problems

community_misconceptions.misconception: You can do a provincial nomination, get PR approved, and then land in Canada for the first time
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Some older immigration pathways allowed overseas applicants to receive PR without prior Canadian presence; immigration companies sometimes still imply this is possible
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: No current provincial nomination program allows land-after-PR; IRCC requires the applicant to have genuinely been working in Canada during the nomination period, and absence during this period flags the job offer's authenticity
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Applications structured this way are flagged for investigation; the job offer's authenticity is questioned, provincial nomination may be revoked, and the federal PR application is rejected

community_misconceptions.misconception: Buying an LMIA job offer adds reliable CRS points and is a standard, safe way to boost scores
community_misconceptions.why_believed: LMIA job offers did historically add CRS points, and the practice was widespread enough to be normalized in Chinese immigration communities; the transactional framing ('buy points') made it feel like a straightforward product
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: As of 2025, IRCC removed LMIA-based CRS score additions. Even before removal, bulk LMIA sellers were flagged by IRCC, and applications linked to known fraudulent employers carried misrepresentation risk for the applicant
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Applicants who purchased LMIA job offers from flagged employers received rejection plus misrepresentation findings, potentially resulting in 5-year bars from Canadian immigration

community_misconceptions.misconception: Low-barrier programs like Atlantic Immigration or caregiver pathways are safer choices for weaker applicants
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Lower minimum requirements feel like lower risk; the logic 'if I barely qualify for the hard program, I should do the easy program' is intuitive
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: IRCC applies heightened scrutiny to low-barrier programs because they attract abuse; Chinese applicants in Atlantic Immigration Program specifically face more rigorous verification of job authenticity and applicant-role fit
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: A weaker applicant with a mismatched profile in a low-barrier program often faces higher practical rejection probability than a strong applicant in a competitive program

real_case_outcomes.situation: Applicant studied 2 years at Ontario college, graduated, obtained 3-year PGWP, then relocated to Manitoba and worked for a Manitoba employer for 1+ year
real_case_outcomes.decision: Applied for Manitoba PNP despite -100 point out-of-province study penalty
real_case_outcomes.outcome: EOI score of 718 (above invitation thresholds), received invitation, submitted materials in June, received provincial nomination in October of same year (~4 months processing), successfully obtained provincial nomination letter
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Out-of-province study penalty is survivable in Manitoba PNP if the 500-point employer continuity bonus is earned; applicants should not be deterred by the penalty from pursuing Manitoba PNP after relocating

real_case_outcomes.situation: Typical Chinese international student profile: under 30, domestic Chinese bachelor's degree, Canadian college diploma, 1-2 years Canadian work experience, IELTS 4x6
real_case_outcomes.decision: Relied solely on federal EE pathway without exploring alternatives
real_case_outcomes.outcome: CRS score approximately 424 — consistently below the 450+ draw thresholds that persisted across all 28 draws observed by the original poster, making federal EE draws essentially inaccessible
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The most common international student profile in Canada is structurally uncompetitive in federal EE all-program draws; alternative pathways (PNP, language improvement, additional credentials) must be considered from the start rather than as fallbacks

psychological_barriers.trigger: Applicant asks 'which immigration program has the lowest requirements I can meet?' without asking about officer scrutiny or profile fit
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Risk minimization through threshold thinking — focusing on getting past the gate rather than on what happens during review; anxiety about being rejected from competitive programs leads to seeking any technically valid option
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Pursuing low-barrier programs (caregiver, Atlantic, provincial entrepreneur) despite obvious profile mismatches; treating minimum eligibility as sufficient
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe: 'Meeting minimum requirements is the entry condition, not the success condition. The question is whether an immigration officer looking at your entire profile will find this application credible. Let's evaluate that.'

psychological_barriers.trigger: Applicant has been in EE pool for months or years without receiving ITA, becomes increasingly desperate for any pathway forward
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Sunk cost + escalating commitment — having invested time in EE makes switching strategies feel like giving up, even when the evidence clearly shows the score is non-competitive
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Continuing to wait in EE pool with sub-450 scores while draw cutoffs remain 490+; becoming vulnerable to exploitative 'guaranteed pathway' sales pitches from immigration companies
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe: 'The time you've spent in the pool is not wasted, but staying in a non-competitive position has a real opportunity cost — your age score is decreasing every year. What would you do differently if you were starting fresh today?'

psychological_barriers.trigger: Applicant who wants to immigrate to Canada is being sold an immigration program by a company that says 'don't worry, we handle everything, many clients have succeeded'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Authority transfer and social proof bias — delegating due diligence to the company because the applicant doesn't have domain expertise, and using other people's claimed success as a proxy for safety
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Paying fees without asking for specific employer names, support letter organization names, or Barrister details; accepting 'we've done hundreds of these' as a sufficient answer
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Provide a concrete set of questions the applicant can ask: 'What is the name of the specific employer / designated organization? What is their track record with IRCC? What happens if the officer questions the application — who handles the appeal and what is their name and background?'

psychological_barriers.trigger: Applicant is evaluating staying in Canada vs. returning to China, and lists domestic China problems (pollution, housing costs, education) as primary reasons to stay
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Push-factor framing and negativity bias about the origin country — immigration decision is being driven by what they're running from rather than a clear-eyed assessment of what they can realistically achieve in Canada
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Committing to any available immigration pathway regardless of fit or risk, because 'I can't go back'; vulnerability to exploitative products because the bar for 'acceptable' is set by fear of the alternative
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe: 'Your motivation to stay is valid. But the question isn't stay-or-go — it's which specific pathway gives you the highest probability of a stable legal status in Canada. Let's focus on what you can actually control.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: I want to immigrate to Canada — which program should I choose?
reframing_moves.reframe: Before asking which program to choose, calculate your actual CRS score and compare it to real draw history; the answer to 'which program' is entirely determined by where your score puts you relative to what's competitive
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts from a product-selection mindset (which the immigration industry exploits) to a data-first diagnostic mindset; forces the applicant to engage with their actual competitive position rather than abstract program descriptions
reframing_moves.example_language: 'The question isn't which program sounds good — it's what your score is and where that puts you in the queue. Everything else follows from that number.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: This immigration company does hundreds of cases per year, so they must be experienced and trustworthy
reframing_moves.reframe: For programs requiring genuine employer matching (LMIA, Atlantic, caregiver, provincial entrepreneur), volume is a red flag not a trust signal — these programs structurally cannot be legitimately batch-processed
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Inverts a cognitive heuristic (scale = competence) that is specifically exploited by fraudulent immigration companies; gives the applicant a concrete counter-signal to act on
reframing_moves.example_language: 'Any company that claims to do hundreds of LMIA job offers per year — ask yourself: where are all these real employers coming from? This isn't a business you can batch-produce.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: I got the provincial nomination letter, so my immigration is basically done
reframing_moves.reframe: Provincial nomination is the halfway point, not the finish line — you still have 1.5-2 years of federal processing ahead, and you need to keep genuinely working in the province throughout
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Corrects a dangerous milestone illusion before the applicant makes decisions (leaving the province, stopping work) that would trigger nomination revocation
reframing_moves.example_language: 'Think of the provincial nomination as getting accepted to university — it's great news, but you still have to show up and do the work, or they take it back.'
